A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UNOT research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–D are readable and support a reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering.

before.justification: v5 reports original experiments on transport prediction, Sinkhorn initialization, barycenters, geodesics, and gradient flows, plus resolution and variable-epsilon experiments in Appendix D.

after.justification: v6 retains original empirical results and adds experiments with additional costs and spherical data, a Meta OT comparison, quantitative barycenter evaluation, and generator-training diagnostics.

M1.justification: v6 introduces a spherical adaptation using SFNOs and the spherical Fourier transform instead of the ordinary Fourier transform (Section 4; Appendix A.5). The adversarial generator, bootstrapping loss, and training algorithm remain. The spectral MLP, fixed-size MLP variant, and variable-epsilon inputs were already documented in v5.

E1.justification: v5 evaluates image distributions on the unit square with squared Euclidean cost. v6 additionally evaluates unsquared Euclidean cost and image distributions projected onto the sphere with spherical distance, training separate models. This substantially expands tested costs and geometries. Cars and Facial Expressions already appeared in v5's appendix.

E2.justification: v5 explicitly excludes direct evaluation against Meta OT. v6 trains that comparator and reports a four-method comparison with UNOT, Gauss, and Ones across six dataset settings in Table 4. Table 6 additionally compares Gauss and Ones against UNOT for barycenter computation; v5 showed barycenters against ground truth without these comparator results.

E3.justification: The stated training-resolution range changes from 28×28–64×64 to 10×10–64×64, including the variable-epsilon variant. New protocols resize all Meta OT comparison data to 28×28 and evaluate barycenter Wasserstein-2 error after 100 gradient steps. These are substantive reported setting additions and revisions; they do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D.6 adds a diagnostic comparing errors on generated samples at their creation and at training completion (Table 5), testing learning across generator stages. Appendix D.7 extends the existing marginal-constraint analysis with single-iteration distributions and additional costs. The resolution and variable-epsilon analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions average experimental errors over 500 samples and already report distributions and mean-plus-dispersion results, including the unchanged entries in Table 1. Additional v6 tables extend this reporting without introducing a new stated uncertainty-estimation procedure, seed count, repeated-run design, or significance test.

E6.justification: v6 adds results for the additional costs and Tables 4–6. Table 4 reports UNOT versus Meta OT errors of 1.3% versus 23.1% on CIFAR at 28×28, while Meta OT remains slightly better on MNIST. Table 6 reports barycenter errors of 0.021, 0.033, and 0.057 for UNOT, Gauss, and Ones. Table 2 replaces the maximum speedup of 3.46× with 7.4×; matching timing conditions are not established.

T1.justification: v6 broadens Proposition 2's cost assumptions to Lipschitz costs, adds Theorem B.3 proving equivalence of pointwise and uniform discretization, and extends Proposition 5's proof to predictions with nonzero mean. Theorem 3 and Corollary 4 are substantively revised around the invertible pre-ReLU residual map, including allowance for lambda equal to one.

C1.justification: The central claims about universal prediction, bootstrapping, and Sinkhorn initialization remain. v6 explicitly includes experiments across costs and Euclidean/non-Euclidean domains in its contributions, raises the headline speedup from 3.46× to 7.4×, and qualifies the generator contribution by fixed dimension.

C2.justification: v6 interprets near-Meta-OT accuracy on MNIST as evidence of generator coverage and adds an interpretation of learning samples from different generator stages. Lower-resolution performance is described as within-range generalization rather than v5's extrapolation claim. The discussion also explicitly identifies non-uniform grids as future work.

D1.justification: v6 supplies explicit complex spectral tensor shapes and multiplication rules, GeLU activations, named optimizers, and clearer batch/minibatch information. It also documents spherical-grid construction, the Meta OT implementation source, and JAX timing conditions including float32, batch size 64, and NVIDIA 4090 hardware. These substantially improve documentation; the UNOT code-and-weights link was already present.

R1.justification: v6 adds references for spherical FNOs, Adam/AdamW, and point-cloud applications by Geuter et al. and Fishman et al. Its main positioning against problem-specific neural OT remains. The Meta OT citation's change from 2022 preprint to 2023 publication is an update to the same work.

P1.justification: The overall section and appendix structure remains. Changes include localized abstract and discussion rewrites, expanded FNO explanations in Section 3.2 and Appendix A.5, moving training details into Section 4, and revised appendix organization. Author affiliations and proceedings information are also updated.

P2.justification: v6 adds spherical examples, plots for additional costs, marginal-constraint distributions, and three result tables. It restructures Table 3 and redraws many charts with changed styling, legends, and scales, including linear rather than logarithmic marginal-constraint plots. Existing barycenter, geodesic, and architecture illustrations are largely retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v6 resolves an important comparison gap by directly evaluating Meta OT, adds quantitative support for previously visual barycenter demonstrations, and tests broader geometries. The new discretization proof and extension of the bootstrapping bound to uncentered predictions strengthen theoretical support, while implementation disclosures improve reproducibility. These gains are substantial independently of the higher speedups, whose changed or previously unspecified timing conditions limit direct before-and-after interpretation.
